profile.summary: This is the autoregressive sequence model released as SeqDesign by Shin and colleagues, which ProteinGym lists as WaveNet. It learns the probability of a protein sequence residue by residue from a set of unaligned family sequences, using a dilated convolutional network rather than a recurrent one. Because it needs no alignment it can score insertions and deletions as well as single substitutions, by comparing the log probability of a mutant sequence with the wild type, and the same trained model can generate new sequences. There is no pretrained checkpoint: a model is trained for each protein family.

summary_quotes.text: SeqDesign is a generative, unsupervised model for biological sequences.

It is capable of learning functional constraints from unaligned sequences
in order to predict the effects of mutations and generate novel sequences,
including insertions and deletions.
we parameterize this process with dilated convolutional neural networks
The model performs state-of-art prediction of missense and indel effects

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model learns the probability of a protein sequence one residue at a time, from unaligned sequences of a protein family. Instead of a recurrent network it uses a residual causal dilated convolutional network: six blocks of nine dilated convolutional layers, with weight normalisation and layer normalisation, dropout at 0.5 after each block and L2 regularisation on the weights. The authors say the number of blocks and layers was chosen to cover protein sequences of any length. To score a variant, the model gives the log probability of the mutant sequence; because no alignment is needed, insertions and deletions can be scored as well as substitutions.

sections.title: How a model is trained and used
sections.body: A model is fitted per protein family: the training input is a FASTA file of that family's sequences, with an optional weight appended to each header, and the README's single command trains it. Prediction then scores a FASTA of variants into a CSV. The README offers two prediction settings: deterministic, with dropout kept at 1.0 and one sample, or an average of 500 samples at dropout 0.5. The same trained model can also generate new sequences. In the paper, six models are built for each family, three replicates in each of the two reading directions, each trained for 250,000 updates with Adam, batch size 30 and channel size 48.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The code has several versions and no single pretrained checkpoint. The branch read here is v3, which the README says works with Python 3 and TensorFlow 1; the v2 branch holds the Python 2.7 code used in the preprint, and a separate PyTorch port is linked. The paper's code availability note gives the repository and a Zenodo deposit. Because a model is trained per family, a reported result has to name the training sequence set, the branch or commit, the reading direction and replicate, and the prediction setting (deterministic or the 500 sample average).

sections.title: How this record was benchmarked
sections.body: The record comes from ProteinGym, whose README lists a baseline called WaveNet, citing this paper, and gives its input modality as MSA. The developers' own sources do not use the name WaveNet: the paper calls the architecture a residual causal dilated convolutional network and the released code is called SeqDesign, which the README describes as learning from unaligned sequences. So ProteinGym gives the input modality as MSA while the developers describe the model as alignment free. The sources read here do not say how ProteinGym prepared that input.

run_guide.summary: Install the package at the pinned commit, train a model on one protein family and score a set of variants.
prerequisites: A GPU with CUDA is recommended, especially for training, per INSTALL.md.
The versions the developers tested: Python 3.7, TensorFlow 1.15, numpy 1.15, scipy 0.19 and sklearn 0.18, on Ubuntu 18.04 LTS.
A FASTA file of the protein family's sequences for training, and a FASTA file of the variant sequences to score.
Training time: the published models were each trained for 250,000 updates, so plan for a long run.

notes: The record is named Wavenet after the ProteinGym baseline table. The developers do not use that name: the released software is SeqDesign and the paper describes a residual causal dilated convolutional network, which is the WaveNet style of architecture. This page therefore treats SeqDesign as the model's own release and says where the name comes from. ProteinGym lists the input modality as MSA while the developers describe the model as alignment free and trained on unaligned family sequences; the sources read here do not resolve how ProteinGym prepared that training input, and a reviewer may want to check the ProteinGym scoring scripts. There are no pretrained weights at all, so weights_licence and weights_url are null and the run guide trains a model. The v2 branch holds the preprint's Python 2.7 code and a separate PyTorch port exists, so a result must say which line it used.
